newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks scale new heights, baht weakens further.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks scale new heights, baht weakens further.

text.p: Thai share prices rose for the third day in a row on Friday, while the Bank of Thailand allowed the baht to weaken further within its new managed float regime.
As signs of profit-taking began to set in on the Thai stock exchange, officials warned that the country's ailing finance sector would make a slow recovery in 1997.

"For the rest of the year we will see slow recovery in the finance sector. We will have a lesser number but stronger finance companies in the next two to three months," Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee told reporters.
Many hope the bitter medicine administered by the Thai government to the economy -- including Wednesday's shock decision to float the baht -- will allow it to recover.
But both analysts and officials warn it will take time before the economy, mired in its worst slump for more than a decade, can be given a clean bill of health.
Thai stocks were up 6.6 percent by midday on Friday, although the rally showed signs of sputtering after leaping from eight-year lows this week.
By 0530 GMT, the key SET index -- which has risen by 17 percent over the past two days -- was up another 40.79 points at 658.77 in heavy trade.
This was off the 667.36 level seen earlier in the day and traders said investors were starting to search for stocks with fundamental value.
"It's been completely mad but it has to come back to fundamentals eventually," said a trader at a European broker.
Traders were waiting to hear whether Stock Exchange officials would widen daily trading limits on share prices, a move which would allow prices to rise -- or fall -- more sharply.
With most blue chips hitting their daily 10 percent trading limits within minutes of opening, investors have been rushing into any available vehicle with which to ride the rally.
Prices on the no-limits foreign board of shares have rocketed 200-300 percent to levels not seen since July 1995.
"It shows that everyone agrees that you buy after a devaluation and not before. There has been a frantic scramble for stock," said Ian Mclennan, head of research at SBC Warburg.
"People are looking around for whatever they can again today," one local trader said.
In the foreign exchange market, business was muted as the baht stabilised near levels reached after losing nearly 20 percent of its value on news of the managed float on Wednesday.
Traders said they would remain firmly on the sidelines after being badly burned by measures taken by the Thai authorities to stem speculation against the baht in the last few weeks.
"I'm not interested at the moment. I'll want to let it all settle down before I go back in," the head of trading at a European bank said.

Since the baht last came under attack in May, coordinated central bank intervention, the imposition of capital controls and a sharp rise in interest rates have made speculators wary of the Thai currency -- despite this week's de facto devaluation.
On Friday, the Bank of Thailand allowed its new daily reference rate for the currency to weaken slightly to 28.189 to the dollar from 27.383 on Thursday.
In the domestic market the baht was trading around 28.650/28.950 to the dollar by 0400 GMT compared to 28.25/28.65 late on Thursday.
Offshore, the currency was quoted around 28.75/29.00 versus 29.00/29.50 late on Thursday.
Dealers and investors were still digesting the change from a 13-year-old system which had pegged the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
The new reference rate is a weighted average of the previous day's trading levels.
